questions.explanation: "Must" takes the base verb and never changes: he must leave now. The -s of the simple present does not go on "must" or on the verb after it, and "must" never takes "to" (only "have to" does).

questions.prompt: Complete: "The bus did not come yesterday, so we ___ walk to school."
questions.explanation: "Yesterday" puts the obligation in the past, and the past of "have to" is "had to": we had to walk to school. "must" has no past form, "have to" is the present and "will have to" is the future.

questions.prompt: A sign at the swimming pool forbids running. Which sentence gives this rule?

options.text: You mustn't run near the pool.
You must run near the pool.
You mustn't to run near the pool.

questions.explanation: Prohibition is "mustn't" + base verb: you mustn't run near the pool. "must" gives the opposite, an obligation; "Don't" takes the base verb (Don't run), never by -ing; and "mustn't" keeps the rules of must, so no "to".

questions.prompt: Someone threw used batteries into the river. Nobody is sure what will happen to the fish. Which sentence fits best?
questions.explanation: Nobody is sure, so the result is only possible: "could" (like may and might) + base verb means perhaps — the fish could die. "must" and "have to" express obligation, and "can't" would say the fish are not able to die.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with "be unable to": "Some old people can't walk without help."

options.text: Some old people is unable to walk without help.
Some old people are unable walk without help.
Some old people are unable to walk without help.
Some old people are unable to walks without help.

questions.explanation: "Can't" becomes "be unable to" + base verb, and "be" agrees with the subject: "some old people" is they, so "are unable to walk". "is" does not agree with a plural subject, "unable" always keeps its "to", and the verb after "to" stays bare.

questions.prompt: Salma has a bad cough. Her friend wants to give her advice. Which sentence does it correctly?

options.text: You ought to see a doctor.

questions.explanation: Advice is "should" or "ought to" + base verb, and "ought" never goes without "to": you ought to see a doctor. "ought see" drops the "to", "mustn't" forbids the visit to the doctor, and "might" only says it is possible.
